recommendation.text: I am responsible for the platform's architecture, and this is my recommendation: one plan, with my reasons, so you can agree with it, change it, or pick differently on the pages that follow. Every figure comes from the estimates behind them.

recommendation.heading: The short version
recommendation.text: MVP 1 is the platform out of the door: the twelve items of the proposal, plus 46.5 hours of your Core list, $3,488, landing about October 26. I have kept it to the basics, and by basics I mean what the platform is wrong or unusable without: who a person is and what they may do in their community, one history that every record writes into, the people and the property behind every charge, the money story your payments launch has to tell, and the few workflows a community uses every week. The rest of your Core list is 27.5 hours and follows as MVP 2, sized on these pages so you can see all of it, with no date on it yet. Every hour on these pages is priced 25% under my estimate.

recommendation.heading: Why the basics, and why in this order
recommendation.text: An HOA platform is built in layers, each one resting on the one below. At the bottom is who the person is and which community they are acting in (roles, scoping). On that sits the record of what happened (the activity and audit trail). On that sit the records themselves: properties, households, owners, tenants, designations. Money sits on the records, because every charge belongs to a property and a person. Only then come the workflows people see. Each layer is what the next one keys on. A workflow built before its records is rebuilt when the records change; a workflow built before the shared history invents its own and never joins the rest. So MVP 1 is not the cheapest set of features, it is the shallowest set that is still whole: every layer present, thin, and correct, with the weekly workflows sitting on top of it rather than beside it.

recommendation.heading: What MVP 1 is
recommendation.text: Foundation (P2, and C1): the HOA Administrator role of its own, the property and community switcher, and several roles for one person. C1 is the one candidate I recommend for the launch, because your first communities are self-managed: their board members are homeowners. Today a homeowner who becomes Treasurer stops being a homeowner in the app. Fixing that later means touching every permission check again; fixing it first costs about 5 hours once. History (P1): the audit record and the activity model, so every workflow that follows records into one history from day one. People and property (P5a, P3): who lives where and in what capacity, and the spreadsheet import and the invitations that get a community in — without those two there is nobody to launch to. Money (P7, P8): delinquency and payment arrangements, and the budget with monthly statements, so the payments launch tells the whole money story: what is owed, what was collected, and what it was spent on. The weekly workflows (P13, P12, P9, P10, P16): notices and alerts, documents with tracking and acknowledgments, the violations rules, maintenance and vendors, and architectural applications and review — what a homeowner and a board actually do between meetings. And the way in and the way out (P4, P17, P18a): account recovery and support access that a community has to permit, the board's own administration screens, and help and contact routes, because in the first week somebody will be locked out and somebody will need to reach a person.

recommendation.heading: What follows as MVP 2
recommendation.text: Sized, ranked, and deliberately without a date: property records in full — status, units, pets and vehicles (P5b); reporting a sale and the ownership handoff, with the title-company access and paid transfer package that follows it (P6a, P6b); votes and surveys (P14); the calendar, contacts, directory, roster and feed (P15b); parking rules and visitor passes (P11b, P11a); and the HOAhx Copilot (P18b), which answers from the document library and so has to come after it and after your decision on its provider. That is 27.5 hours, $2,063. None of it is dropped: every item is on the Features page with its hours, and a sale or a vote in the first weeks is handled the way it is handled today while MVP 1 proves itself.

recommendation.heading: What I would leave for later, and why
recommendation.text: The management-company items (C5, C6, and the transition case) serve an audience the brand foundation puts after the launch; self-managed communities come first. The fuller versions on the Declined sheet (the vendor marketplace, the technician route, the photo gallery, meetings as a workflow) are products in their own right on top of features that do not exist yet. Modules & Features (C7) gates features; it is cheaper to add gates to a finished set than to build gates and features together. Passkeys (D-216) and the page-routing upgrade (D-217) are worthwhile, but each touches every sign-in or every screen: do them between releases, not during one.

recommendation.heading: What this asks of you
recommendation.text: Say yes to MVP 1 as it stands, or move packages in or out of it on the Packages page; the total, the date and the cost move with your picks. Two decisions are yours alone and are on the register: the Copilot's provider, and whether several roles for one person is in the launch. If you say nothing else, I build in the order on the Build order column and stop where the hours you approve run out.

inScope.title: Access ends at once when a person's last role is removed
inScope.adds: A clear 'your access was removed' screen instead of actions failing until the session expires.
inScope.today: The cached session lasts until the sign-in token refreshes (up to an hour) or the page reloads; then scoped actions fail, and a reload sends a person with no communities to the join page. There is no 'your access was removed' screen.

inScope.title: Sign-in links only return to HOAhx pages
inScope.adds: A same-site check on every return address, so a crafted link cannot send a signed-in person elsewhere.
inScope.today: The return address on a sign-in link is followed as given; the routing library's fix needs a major upgrade across every screen.

inScope.title: Tenant access: invitations, what a tenant may see and do, owner visibility into tenant requests, expiry and renewal, and default exclusions
inScope.adds: Tenant invitations with the owner choosing access to notices, requests, amenities, parking, and visitor functions, owner visibility into the tenant's permitted requests, an end date with authorized renewal, and the exclusions on by default.
inScope.today: An owner invites a tenant and chooses at invitation whether the tenant may see announcements, receive notifications, reserve amenities, use parking, and view documents (finance access is separate and always enforced); the parking and amenity choices are honored only in the menus, the documents choice has no effect, changes after the invitation do not save, a lease end date can be recorded but does not end access, and an owner cannot see the tenant's requests.

inScope.title: "Where does my money go?": the approved budget shown to homeowners, with source, period, update date, and budget versus actual
inScope.adds: A homeowner view of the published budget: the dues split by category as a chart with amounts and shares, the approved budget named as the source with its period and last update, and a budget-versus-actual table for the same period, with the demo's plain notes about what the figures mean.
inScope.today: The board builds and publishes a budget on an administrator-only screen; homeowners see the published budget's category split on their payments screen (a dashboard card meant to show it never loads) with no source, period, or update date; the board has a budget-versus-actual report, homeowners do not.

inScope.title: Staff-only notes kept out of the record the resident reads
inScope.adds: Only the resident concerned and the authorized roles see a violation; internal notes move out of the resident-visible record.
inScope.today: Only the subject and authorized staff can see a violation.

inScope.title: Violations: community-configured categories and procedures, property or vehicle association, evidence and notice dates, draft notices, homeowner acknowledgment and response, and correction photos
inScope.adds: Categories with their procedure and deadlines, draft notices reviewed before sending, an acknowledgment and a response from the homeowner, and correction photos that move the case toward resolution.
inScope.today: Administrators issue notices with photos, track status, and apply fees; residents can file a report, but reports reach nobody; the homeowner can reply in writing, submit a written cure statement, or appeal with up to three files; there is no configured procedure per category, no draft notice, no acknowledgment step, and no correction-photo submission.

inScope.title: Disputes and hearing requests, fine and escalation visibility, administrative verification and final resolution, and a complete history in neutral language
inScope.adds: A dispute and hearing request on every notice, fine and escalation visible to the homeowner and authorized roles, an administrator's verification before a case closes, and a history in plain, neutral wording.
inScope.today: A case can be escalated through fees to a lien and carries an appeal-pending state; a re-inspection with a pass or fail finding exists after a cure but is not required before a case is resolved; there is no hearing request; the full history is recorded but the homeowner sees only a three-step status, not the record.

inScope.title: Visitor passes with validity dates and active, scheduled, expired, and revoked status
inScope.adds: A visitor pass with a validity window, a code the guest presents, and a status that moves from scheduled to active to expired or revoked, sent to the guest by the homeowner. Extending a visit, a recurring schedule, and the guest's own arrival view are in the launch as their own entries (D-199, D-200, D-207).
inScope.today: Visitors are authorized by name with an optional start and end date and show as active, expired, or revoked (a visit that has not started yet still shows as active); the community keeps a visitor log; the visitor gets no code and nothing is sent to them, although a separate guest parking pass does carry a code valid for up to three days.

inScope.title: Targeting by community, role, property, or group; templates, scheduled messages, drafts, and autosave; delivery, failure, and read status where measurable
inScope.adds: Targeting by role, property, and group, saved templates, scheduled sends, drafts that autosave, and delivery and failure status per message with read status where the channel reports it.
inScope.today: Mass communications reach every resident's in-app notice list (not their email) with a recipient preview, a history, and a per-channel delivery status; the board can target residents only, a role, a building, a unit type, or a delinquency status; saved message templates exist but are not offered on the send screen; there is no scheduling, no draft, and no read status; announcements track reads.

inScope.title: Quorum as a percentage of entitled properties
inScope.adds: Every formal vote requires a quorum from the community's rules, with no default of one; a vote without quorum is recorded as failed.
inScope.today: Quorum is set per vote as a number of weighted ballots and defaults to one, so unless the board raises it when creating the vote, a single ballot meets quorum. It is not a percentage of owners.

inScope.title: Surveys: question types, drafts, dates, reminders, eligible audiences, identified or anonymous responses, participation and results with exports, and resident access to active and past surveys
inScope.adds: The five question types, drafts, scheduled open and close, reminders, audiences by role or property, participation tracking, results with an export, and past surveys visible by rule.
inScope.today: Surveys are published at creation or saved as a draft that cannot be published afterwards; residents answer once, an anonymous option exists, and there are three question types (multiple choice, a one-to-five rating, written); there are no scheduled dates, reminders, audiences, exports, or resident access to past surveys.

inScope.title: Amenities: listings, rules, availability, capacity, and eligibility; direct booking or approval; hours and blackout dates; confirmations, reminders, cancellations, and schedule management; no double bookings; tenant eligibility and access expiry
inScope.adds: Reservations for every listed amenity with rules, hours, blackouts, approval where the community wants it, confirmations, reminders, cancellation, conflict prevention, and eligibility that follows tenant access and its expiry. A single Amenity Pass is in the launch as its own entry (D-201).
inScope.today: Only the clubhouse can be reserved (with an access log and a code shown on approval) and the dog park has check-ins; the amenity list with hours, capacity, and rules is visible to administrators only, and its switches for reservations and approval change nothing; a property owner can switch a tenant's reservation, guest, and history access on and off but only the screen honours it; blackout dates and reminders are not built.

inScope.title: One Amenity Pass with temporary access
inScope.adds: A pass per reservation with a temporary code, where the amenity has compatible access hardware.
inScope.today: An approved clubhouse reservation already shows the resident a code image and a short access code, and check-in writes an access log; the code is not time-limited and opens nothing by itself.
